summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: A social worker and police officer may enter a home without a warrant to check on children reported abused only if the officer is actually motivated by a need to render aid and, objectively, a reasonable person would have believed an emergency existed.
key_cases.relevance: It supplies the exigency test that legitimizes taking a child into protective custody without prior judicial authorization.
key_cases.quote: Both tests must be satisfied before a warrantless entry will be justified under the emergency rule exception.

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel. Angela M.W. v. Kruzicki
key_cases.holding: The definition of 'child' in Wis. Stat. sec. 48.02(2) does not include a viable fetus, so the juvenile court had no Children's Code jurisdiction to take a pregnant woman into custody to protect her fetus.
key_cases.relevance: It marks the outer jurisdictional limit of protective custody under ch. 48.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the definition of "child" in § 48.02(2) does not include a viable fetus

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: A Racine County caseworker who removed a child on neglect allegations was entitled to qualified immunity because a reasonable caseworker could have believed probable cause existed, and no evidence showed that probable cause dissipated before the court's probable-cause order two days later.
key_cases.relevance: It confirms that taking a child into protective custody is a Fourth Amendment seizure needing court order, probable cause, or exigency.
key_cases.quote: However, the continued withholding of a minor may constitute a constitutional violation where probable cause or reasonable suspicion dissipates.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: A child removed from his home on knowingly false allegations of neglect, without investigation, a pre-deprivation hearing, or exigent circumstances, states Fourth Amendment, substantive and procedural due process claims under sec. 1983 against the officials involved.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that taking a child into custody for questioning, without parental consent, is a seizure.
key_cases.quote: at a minimum it requires that government officials not misrepresent the facts in order to obtain the removal of a child from his parents

key_cases.case_name: Hernandez ex rel. Hernandez v. Foster
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: A child's initial removal supported by probable cause is reasonable, but continuing to hold the child in protective custody after probable cause and reasonable suspicion have dissipated states Fourth Amendment and substantive due process claims that survive qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Seventh Circuit's fullest statement that protective custody is a continuing seizure that must remain justified for as long as it lasts.
key_cases.quote: Nor does it suggest that the state may retain custody of a child for up to forty-eight hours where probable cause and even reasonable suspicion no longer exist.

state_agency.name: Wisconsin Department of Children and Families
state_agency.hotline: No statewide hotline. Call the county or tribal agency where the child lives — the list is at dcf.wisconsin.gov/reportabuse

mandatory_reporters: Physicians, naturopathic doctors, nurses, dentists, chiropractors, optometrists, acupuncturists, and medical or mental health professionals not otherwise specified (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)1., 1m., 4.–9.)
Social workers, marriage and family therapists, and professional counselors (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)10.–12.)
Public assistance workers, including financial and employment planners (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)13.)
School teachers, school administrators, school counselors, and school employees not otherwise specified (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)14.–16., 16m.)
Child care workers in a child care center, group home, or residential care center for children and youth, and child care providers (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)18., 19.)
Alcohol or other drug abuse counselors and genetic counselors (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)20., 20m.)

Treatment staff employed by or working under contract with a county department under Wis. Stat. § 46.23, 51.42, or 51.437, or with a residential care center for children and youth (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)21.)
Physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, occupational therapists, and dietitians (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)22., 22m., 23., 24.)
Emergency medical services practitioners and emergency medical responders (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)27., 28.)
Police or law enforcement officers and juvenile correctional officers (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)29., 30.)
Court-appointed special advocates, as to children seen in the course of activities under Wis. Stat. § 48.236(3) (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(b))
Members of the clergy, except for child abuse information received solely through confidential communications made privately or in a confessional setting (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(bm)1.–3.)
Any other person, including an attorney — permissive only; may report but is not required to (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(c))

notice_requirements.timing: Within 24 hours after a county department that has a federally recognized reservation or the Ho-Chunk service area wholly or partly within its county receives a report about a child it knows or has reason to know is an Indian child residing in the county, or an Indian unborn child whose expectant mother resides in the county
content_required: Name and address of the Indian child or expectant mother
The fact that a report has been received about that Indian child or Indian unborn child

statutory_basis.citation_text: Wis. Stat. § 48.981(3)(bm) (notice of report to Indian tribal agent)
